hero.headline: Two Martin County brush fires contained, more expected this summer
hero.teaser: Martin County saw two brush fires this week, including one sparked by a lightning strike, both now fully contained and being monitored by the Florida Forest Service.
hero.body:
Two brush fires broke out in Martin County this week, including one ignited by a lightning strike, and both are now fully contained and under monitoring by the Florida Forest Service. Officials are warning that conditions favorable for brush fires will continue throughout the summer months as the region remains in peak fire season.

 David Grubitch, a mitigation specialist and spokesperson with the Florida Forest Service, said summertime heat is drying out fine dead fuels, making them highly receptive when lightning strikes occur. However, he emphasized that residents should not be alarmed by these conditions, as they are typical for this time of year. Grubitch explained that while rain often extinguishes fires immediately after they start, some fires can travel underground and resurface days later, making them more difficult to detect and contain.

 The Florida Forest Service is relying on public assistance to help monitor and respond to brush fires quickly. Grubitch stressed that residents play a crucial role in helping the department do its job effectively and urged people to never assume someone else has already reported a brush fire they spot. He emphasized the importance of immediate notification, saying that if residents see something, they should say something, as it can make all the difference in how quickly crews are able to get a fire under control. Quick reporting remains one of the most effective tools in preventing small fires from becoming larger, more dangerous blazes that threaten homes and natural areas.

 With summer conditions expected to continue creating favorable environments for brush fires, the Florida Forest Service will maintain its heightened monitoring and response efforts throughout the season. The department continues to track contained fires and remains prepared to respond to new incidents as they arise. Residents are encouraged to remain vigilant and report any signs of smoke or fire to local authorities immediately, regardless of whether they believe others may have already called it in. Officials stress that multiple reports of the same fire are preferable to a fire going unreported and potentially spreading out of control.

cards.headline: Treasure Coast reports 3 cyclospora cases as residents avoid lettuce, berries during outbreak
cards.teaser: Health officials confirmed five local cases of cyclospora since May, including two in St. Lucie County and one in Martin County. Families across the Treasure Coast are avoiding leafy greens and switching to alternatives like melons and bananas.
cards.body:
Health officials confirmed five local cases of cyclospora since May, with two in Palm Beach County, two in St. Lucie County and one in Martin County, according to the Florida Department of Health. The concern stems from outbreaks tied to contaminated produce, including lettuce connected to Taco Bell locations, that can cause severe stomach illness and intense diarrhea.

 Thousands across the U.S. have been affected. At restaurants, grocery stores and fast-food chains, families say they are steering clear of leafy greens. George Lorenz said he is taking precautions while grabbing lunch with his father, Brian, on Clematis Street in West Palm Beach, opting for pizza from Elisabetta's instead. In Boynton Beach, Hendriette Peckens said she bought two big bags of oranges, bread and some apples, and planned to cook Alaskan salmon for dinner.

 Samantha Barone, dietitian for the bariatric program at Delray Medical Center, said consumers should focus on produce with protective outer layers. Barone recommends foods like bananas, melons and avocados, noting that consumers should still wash them before cutting into them and peeling them. She also recommends washing all fruits and vegetables thoroughly before eating them and says beans and nuts are safe alternatives that still provide fiber and protein.

 Barone warns to avoid bagged lettuce if possible and recommends buying whole heads of lettuce and peeling away the outer layers. She advises avoiding berries, especially raspberries, because they are difficult to clean properly.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound couple seeks support as husband battles head and neck cancer
cards.teaser: Dave and Faren Motz of Hobe Sound are asking for community support as Dave battles head and neck cancer, facing nearly $20,000 in out-of-pocket costs for treatment.
cards.body:
A Hobe Sound couple is asking for community support as they navigate a cancer diagnosis. Dave and Faren Motz met in South Florida before moving to Maui, where they married and raised their family. Faren homeschooled all three of their children, and the family started a farm where they served children. Years later, the couple moved to Hobe Sound and purchased a property, but just months after settling in, Dave was diagnosed with head and neck cancer.

 As the couple searched for healthcare in Florida, AdventHealth in Celebration provided programs and grants that became a critical resource. Dave underwent nearly seven weeks of daily radiation treatments. The repeated visits to Orlando, biopsies, scans, and exams added up, costing the couple nearly $20,000 out of pocket.

 Their age and income kept them from qualifying for Medicare or Medicaid. Dave, a former firefighter who had long been the family's provider, now has an 85% chance of recovery according to doctors. Faren now works to support them both at Latitudes at the Jupiter Beach Resort, where those who want to show support can visit. Those who would like to contribute financially can donate to the family's GoFundMe at Standing with Dave Motz in his cancer battle.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County man leads Martin County deputies on 100 mph chase through Indiantown
cards.teaser: Markell Tillman, 33, drove more than 100 mph on State Road 710 before leading deputies on a high-speed chase through Indiantown and onto SW Martin Highway toward Palm City.
cards.body:
A Palm Beach County man led Martin County deputies on a high-speed chase through Indiantown after driving more than 100 mph on State Road 710, one of the area's most dangerous roads. Deputies spotted 33-year-old Markell Tillman driving aggressively at speeds exceeding 100 mph, forcing other vehicles off the roadway. When deputies attempted to stop him, Tillman fled. Tillman weaved through traffic in an attempt to lose deputies before turning onto SW Martin Highway toward Palm City, where he continued to drive recklessly.

 Deputies spotted Tillman again traveling eastbound on Martin Highway near Allapattah Road. Deputies used stop sticks to disable his vehicle near I-95. Tillman then bailed out of the vehicle and attempted to flee on foot before deputies caught up with him and took him into custody.

 Tillman was arrested on charges including fleeing and eluding, aggravated fleeing with injury or damage, operating a vehicle exceeding the speed limit by 50 or more mph, driving while license suspended or revoked, obstruction without violence, and operating a vehicle at 100 or more mph. Tillman also had an out-of-county warrant at the time of his arrest. He was booked into the Martin County Jail.

cards.headline: Safe Kids Treasure Coast offering free pool alarms to Martin County residents

 The program offers one alarm per household and has no income or priority group requirements, making it available to any qualifying resident regardless of financial status. The alarms are available while supplies last on a first-come, first-served basis, so interested residents should act promptly to secure one. Safe Kids Treasure Coast is asking residents to fill out an online survey to determine their eligibility for the program.  The initiative aims to increase water safety awareness and provide practical tools to help prevent drowning incidents in residential pools throughout Martin County. By distributing these alarms at no cost, the program seeks to remove financial barriers that might otherwise prevent families from implementing additional safety measures around their pools. cards.body:

The project includes reconstruction of buildings destroyed in the tornadoes, along with a new administration building, media center, art lab, and a full overhaul of the parking lot. The demolition phase alone costs $3.3 million, though the total project cost has not been finalized.

 The project is being funded by local capital improvement, sales tax and Public Education Capital Outlay. Students who were displaced from the affected classrooms will continue learning in portable classrooms until construction is complete.

 Kirstie Gernaine, coordinator of public information and community relations for the Martin County School District, said the school was already scheduled for significant construction before the hurricane struck. "Murray Middle School was already slated to get all of this construction work with a new admin area, a new media center and a brand new art lab," said Gernaine.

 "With Hurricane Milton and those tornadoes destroying the buildings in the back buildings 18, 10, and nine we were able to add these on." The school district said parents can be assured their students will be safe during construction. Barriers have already been placed around the work zone to keep students out. The district hopes to complete the renovations by December 2027.

hero.teaser: Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County is challenging the St. Lucie County Fire District's decision to terminate three firefighters and suspend two others for incidents in 2024.
hero.body:
Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County, IAFF Local 1377, said the St. Lucie County Fire District wrongly terminated and suspended the five members for their involvement in incidents that occurred in March and September 2024. These incidents did not involve any hazing, Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp stated in a letter obtained by WPTV. Sapp pointed to the Fort Pierce Police Department's report, which he said described the situation, in part, as "found coworkers entertaining each other." Sapp also noted that members involved in the incidents were treated differently during the investigative and disciplinary processes, with some receiving no discipline at all.

Local 1377 has demanded arbitration for all five members. The union raised concerns about the outside law firm the fire district hired to conduct its investigation, Allen, Norton & Blue. Local 1377 and its legal counsel said the investigation was not conducted in an impartial or unbiased manner. Sapp stated that the nature of the questions asked reflects a predetermined conclusion rather than an objective fact-finding process. Sapp noted that the same firm that conducted the investigation has since been hired by the fire district to represent it at arbitration. The union said it remains willing to negotiate a resolution that would avoid the significant costs of arbitration, but Sapp said Fire Chief Jeff Lee has not offered any concessions or proposed resolutions.

cards.headline: Double fatal shooting in Port St. Lucie stemmed from jealousy over woman, police say
cards.teaser: Two Fort Pierce men died after an exchange of gunfire early Sunday in the 1300 block of Southeast Rivergreen Circle in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
The double fatal shooting occurred at about 3:30 a.m. Sunday in the 1300 block of Southeast Rivergreen Circle. When officers arrived, they found two men with multiple gunshot wounds in the driveways of a residence. Both victims, identified as Carl Loubeau, 24, and Juliun Stokes, 22, both from Fort Pierce, were taken to separate local hospitals, where they later died from their injuries. Police said a verbal altercation occurred outside the residence over a key to a home and escalated into an exchange of gunfire between two of the individuals involved.

Chief Leo Niemczyk said a woman contacted Loubeau, whom she was dating, for a key because she was locked out of her home. When Carl arrives, he finds her present with other people, including two males, Niemczyk said. The motive behind the initial attack was jealousy over the female. Police said Loubeau was the primary aggressor in the dispute, with Dwayne Walker, 20, discharging his firearm in self-defense. Carl approached Juliun, opened fire on him; apparently, we think he mistook Juliun for Dwayne, starting firing on him, Niemczyk said. Dwayne was in close proximity and withdrew his firearm, which is lawfully carried, and started firing on Carl. Niemczyk said their current investigation shows that Loubeau fired eight rounds from a 9 mm pistol and one round from a .380 pistol, with Walker firing eight rounds from his .40 caliber pistol. Police said Walker was not injured in the incident. No arrests have been made in the case.

cards.headline: New tuition-free tech school in Fort Pierce to combine academics with career training
cards.teaser: SouthTech Treasure Coast will open in Fort Pierce in August, offering middle and high school students the opportunity to earn industry certifications while completing traditional coursework.
cards.body:
SouthTech Treasure Coast will give middle and high school students the opportunity to earn industry certifications while completing their traditional coursework, helping them build real-world skills and prepare for high-demand careers before they graduate. The tuition-free career and technical charter school is preparing to open in Fort Pierce in August. "All of our students are working on their academics, but they are also all in one of our career academies where they have the opportunity to earn adult level industry certifications while they are still in high school," said Carla Lovett, Executive Director of SouthTech Schools. Nicole Handy, Director of Expansion of SouthTech Schools, said school leaders selected the Treasure Coast because of the area's growing demand for skilled workers.

The St. Lucie County School Board approved the charter application for the Fort Pierce campus in April. The Fort Pierce campus will serve students in grades 6 through 12, with plans to enroll about 460 students in its first year. Students will have the opportunity to choose from career academies including medical science, culinary arts, cosmetology, and agriculture technology. SouthTech Treasure Coast will host a grand opening celebration on Saturday, July 25, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., giving families and community members a chance to tour the new campus and learn more about the programs being offered. SouthTech Treasure Coast in Fort Pierce is located at 2810 S. US Highway 1 Fort Pierce, FL 34982.

cards.body:
Concerns over contaminated produce linked to E. coli and cyclospora outbreaks are prompting South Florida residents to reconsider their food choices, with some avoiding leafy greens entirely. The outbreaks have affected thousands nationwide and include lettuce connected to Taco Bell locations. Health officials have confirmed local cases stretching from the Palm Beaches to the Treasure Coast, including two cases in St. Lucie County.

 The Florida Department of Health reported five confirmed local cases of cyclospora since May. Two cases were reported in Palm Beach County, two in St. Lucie County, and one in Martin County. The contamination concerns have led families across the region to change their eating habits at restaurants, grocery stores, and fast-food chains.

 Dakota and Brynlee Rhodes, who were visiting Delray Beach with their mother Jenny, said they are trying to stay away from lettuce and stuff like that. Other families are similarly steering clear of leafy greens altogether as reports of contaminated produce continue to spread across the country. The widespread nature of the outbreaks has left many consumers uncertain about which products are safe to purchase and consume.

 Samantha Barone, a dietitian for the bariatric program at Delray Medical Center, offered guidance for consumers looking to maintain healthy diets while avoiding potentially contaminated produce. Barone recommends sticking to melon and things that have a harder skin that you can peel. She advises consumers to focus on produce with protective outer layers and to wash all fruits and vegetables thoroughly before eating them.

 For those seeking alternatives to leafy greens, Barone suggests that beans and nuts are safe options that still provide fiber and protein. She specifically recommends cleaning produce using a mixture of one part distilled white vinegar to three parts water. The outbreaks have highlighted the importance of proper food handling and preparation practices for consumers across South Florida.

cards.headline: Two men killed in early morning shooting on Southeast Rivergreen Circle in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: Carl Loubeau, 24, and Juliun Stokes, 22, died Sunday morning after a dispute over a residential key escalated into gunfire.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police responded around 3:30 a.m. Sunday to the 1300 block of Southeast Rivergreen Circle after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting gunshots.

 When officers arrived, they found two adult men suffering from multiple gunshot wounds in the driveways of a residence. Both victims were taken to separate local hospitals, where they later died from their injuries. Police identified the victims as Carl Loubeau, 24, and Juliun Stokes, 22.

 Preliminary investigators believe some of the people involved had been socializing earlier in the evening before returning to a home on Southeast Rivergreen Circle. Police said a verbal altercation occurred outside the residence over a residential key and escalated into an exchange of gunfire between two of the individuals involved. The investigation remains active as detectives continue conducting interviews, processing evidence and reviewing available information. Police said additional details, including any potential criminal charges, will be released as the investigation progresses.

 Neighbor John Adams told WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache he was awake working in his garage when the shooting occurred. "I was just working on my bicycle and I heard gunshots. Maybe two, three and I stayed in the garage and then I heard a girl screaming," Adams said.

 He described a massive emergency response to the scene. "Every police officer in Port St. Lucie was here, there was twenty squads, two ambulances, two firetrucks, a helicopter.

 It was just mayhem," Adams said. He added that a police officer told him they took a picture of 16 casings. "Just devastating, terrible.

 My heart goes out to them," Adams said. Another neighbor who did not want to be identified told WPTV she dialed 911 and stayed with one of the wounded men until help arrived.

 Investigators believe the shooting was an isolated incident involving people who knew one another and said there is no ongoing threat to the public. All parties involved have either been detained or are cooperating with investigators, according to police. Anyone with information who has not yet spoken with detectives is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department.

hero.headline: JetBlue ending Vero Beach to New York JFK route in September due to low demand

hero.body:
JetBlue is canceling its flight route between Vero Beach Regional Airport and New York's JFK Airport, with the last flights operating in September. The airline cited low demand as the reason for ending the route, which launched last December to excitement from Treasure Coast residents hoping for convenient travel options to the Northeast. Brandon Dambeck, interim airport director, said the decision reflects how the airline industry operates based on passenger numbers.

 "It's just the way that that market works, and air carriers will fluctuate based off of demand," Dambeck said. He added that JetBlue "just wasn't seeing what they were hoping for" with the New York route.

 Not everyone agrees the route had a fair shot at success. Charlie Ahern, who regularly uses JetBlue flights at Vero Beach Regional Airport, said he believes the route would have grown over time if given more opportunity. "I think if they hung in there, it would have worked.

 I think it would have built up pretty good," Ahern said. He noted the convenience of flying out of Vero Beach, saying, "It's easy. It's close." His comments reflect concerns from local travelers who appreciated having direct access to New York without driving to larger airports in South Florida or Orlando.

 The Boston route continues to perform well at Vero Beach Regional Airport, with Dambeck saying "Boston is seeing great demand." Grece Ezzi flew into Vero Beach on JetBlue from Boston on Friday for the first time, demonstrating continued interest in that northeastern connection. The contrast between the two routes highlights how different markets can perform differently even when serving similar geographic regions. While both Boston and New York are major northeastern cities, the Boston service has attracted enough passengers to remain viable while the JFK route struggled to build a sustainable customer base.

 Dambeck said the door is not closed on the JFK route returning in the future, noting "They'll evaluate continuously. So just because it's gone now doesn't mean that it never will come back." This leaves open the possibility that JetBlue could restore service to New York if conditions change or demand increases. Airlines regularly reassess their route networks based on seasonal patterns, economic conditions, and shifting travel preferences. For now, Vero Beach travelers seeking to reach New York will need to connect through other cities or use alternative airports.

cards.headline: Indian River County families can apply for free or reduced-price student meals starting July 15
cards.teaser: Families in Indian River County are able to apply for free or reduced price meals for students starting July 15.
cards.body:
Families in Indian River County can apply for free or reduced-price meals for students starting July 15 through the district's online portal. While six schools in the county will automatically provide free meals to all students during the 2026-2027 school year through federal nutrition programs, other families may still qualify based on household size and income levels.

 The application process begins at www.LINQConnect.com, where parents must either sign in to an existing account or create a new one. After logging in, families should search for Indian River County Public Schools in Vero Beach and add their student to the application using the Student ID number and the child's formal name as it appears in FOCUS, the district's student information system. The application can be accessed from the website homepage by clicking School Services at the top menu and then selecting Free and Reduced Meal Application.

 District officials are encouraging families to submit one application per household to determine eligibility. The application requires families to provide information about household size and income to determine eligibility for the federal nutrition programs. By submitting a single application for all children in the household, families can streamline the process and find out if they qualify for free meals, reduced-price meals, or neither option. The program is designed to ensure that students have access to nutritious meals during the school day regardless of their family's financial situation.

 Families who have questions about the meal programs or need assistance with the application process can contact Shawn O'Keefe, the district's nutrition services director. O'Keefe can be reached by phone at (772) 564-5041 or by email at shawn.okeefe@indianriverschools.org. District officials recommend that families apply as early as possible to ensure their eligibility status is determined before the start of the 2026-2027 school year.

cards.body:
JetBlue is ending its direct flights between New York's JFK Airport and Vero Beach Regional Airport, citing low passenger demand for the route that launched in December. The airline announced that service between the two airports will end Sept. 9, just nine months after the route began operating with much fanfare and optimistic passengers. JetBlue said in a statement that demand for this new route has not materialized as the airline had hoped. JetBlue will continue serving Vero Beach through its Boston route and has not announced whether it plans to add any replacement routes from Vero Beach or if it will adjust frequency on the remaining Boston service.

 All affected customers will be notified directly by JetBlue and will receive full refunds. Passengers with upcoming reservations on the discontinued route are encouraged to contact JetBlue directly or check their email for rebooking options and refund information. The JFK-Vero Beach route was seen as a major win for the Treasure Coast when it launched in December 2025, providing direct access to one of the nation's busiest airports and potentially boosting tourism to the area. The inaugural flight brought enthusiastic passengers who called the service a game changer for connecting family and friends between New York and the Treasure Coast.

 The route's cancellation comes as a disappointment to local officials and residents who had hoped the direct connection would strengthen ties between the two regions. The discontinuation of the JFK route after such a short period highlights the challenges smaller regional airports face in sustaining air service to major hubs. While JetBlue's Boston service will continue to provide some connectivity for Vero Beach travelers, the loss of direct access to JFK eliminates what many saw as a crucial link to the New York metropolitan area. The airline has not indicated whether it might reconsider the route in the future or explore other destinations from Vero Beach Regional Airport.

 The route had been viewed as important infrastructure for the region when it first began operations, with hopes that convenient access to JFK would help strengthen economic and personal connections between the Treasure Coast and the New York metropolitan area. The short lifespan of the route underscores the difficulties regional airports encounter when trying to establish and maintain service to major transportation hubs.

cards.headline: Vero Beach parents sue city over infant son's remains allegedly disturbed and reburied without consent
cards.teaser: Adam Chrzan and Tanya Crovo allege their infant son's remains were disturbed during maintenance at Crestlawn Cemetery and reinterred without their knowledge.
cards.body:
Adam Chrzan and Tanya Crovo have filed an amended lawsuit against the City of Vero Beach alleging their infant son's remains were disturbed during maintenance work at Crestlawn Cemetery and reburied without their knowledge or consent. The couple's son, identified in court documents only as A.C., died in August 2007 at 37 days old and was buried at the city-owned cemetery. The parents say they did not learn about what allegedly happened until April 2025, nearly 18 years after their son's burial.

 According to the complaint, sometime between the 2007 burial and April 2025, heavy equipment being used for maintenance or irrigation work near the burial site breached the grave, damaging or destroying the casket, its contents, and the child's remains. The lawsuit alleges that someone acting in an official capacity for the City of Vero Beach then directed cemetery workers to collect the remains, place them into a new casket, and reinter the child without notifying the parents or obtaining their consent. The amended complaint accuses the city and cemetery of tortious interference with a burial plot and human remains, negligence, negligent infliction of emotional distress, intentional misrepresentation, and fraudulent concealment.

 This amended complaint comes after a judge dismissed the family's original lawsuit. The dismissal was not a finding that the allegations were false but rather a ruling that the legal claims as originally pleaded could not proceed against the city under Florida law. The parents have now refiled with different legal arguments in an attempt to overcome the previous dismissal. A judge has not yet ruled on the amended complaint. The City of Vero Beach has declined to comment on the amended complaint.

 In court filings responding to the original lawsuit, the city disputed the allegation that irrigation work could have caused the damage described by the parents. The city submitted a survey stating there are no irrigation lines adjacent to the burial plot of A.C. The case highlights the legal protections cities have under Florida law and the challenges families face when seeking accountability for alleged mishandling of cemetery operations. The amended complaint represents the parents' continued effort to hold the city responsible for what they describe as the unauthorized disturbance and reburial of their infant son's remains.

cards.headline: Decomposed body found near U.S. Highway 1 near Sebastian, second in area this week
cards.teaser: A heavily decomposed body was discovered Wednesday afternoon along the shoreline near 14510 U.S. Highway 1 near Sebastian, the second body found in the area this week.
cards.body:
A caller reported finding a heavily decomposed body in shrubbery along the shoreline near 14510 U.S. Highway 1 near Sebastian shortly after 4 p.m. Wednesday afternoon. The discovery prompted a death investigation by the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. The body was located on the east side of U.S. Highway 1, across the street from where the body of James Thompson was found Monday.

 Detectives and Crime Scene Unit personnel are processing the area and working to identify the deceased. Investigators are working to determine whether the two deaths are related or are separate, unconnected incidents occurring in the same general area. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Indian River County Sheriff's Office or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers to remain anonymous.

cards.body:
New research has focused on Indian River County schools and the district's approach to reversing enrollment declines in the expanding school choice era. The case study explores strategies the district is implementing to attract and retain students.

 Indian River County schools face enrollment challenges as families have more educational options through charter schools, vouchers, and other school choice programs. The research documents how district officials are working to compete in this changed landscape.

 The case study provides insight into the specific tactics Indian River County is employing to stabilize and grow enrollment. School choice expansion has created competitive pressure on traditional public school districts across Florida, making enrollment management a priority for district leadership.

 District administrators are responding to the competitive environment created by increased educational alternatives available to families. The research examines the approaches being taken to address declining student numbers as more parents choose options outside traditional public schools.
